utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, madam registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Today is Tuesday. My greetings to all the people in the courtroom, the OTP representatives, the Defence counsel, the accused, and all the people helping us out. I'll first give the floor to the registrar. She has two IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution response to Exhibits tendered through Witness EA by the accused Stojic, Praljak, Petkovic and Coric will become Exhibit IC 727, and Petkovic Defence objection to the Prosecution list of exhibits tendered through Witness EA will become Exhibit IC 728.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Kovacic wanted to say something, so he has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't be taking up too much time, at least I hope not. We discussed this, the plans and the scheduling and calendar amongst the Defence teams following your recent ruling for the January scheduling, and we noticed that in fact we're not quite sure when in December we're adjourning before the winter break, and that's of course necessary for us to plan our -- to make our travelling arrangements for the winter. So might the Trial Chamber perhaps with the assistance of the Prosecution tell us how long we're going to work in December and when we break for the recess. We're not quite clear on that. And yesterday we received a table with the documents for Witness Ribicic, where the -- well, it was implied that the Prosecution would need four and a half hours for the examination-in-chief. So he can't be over by the 11th, and I hope that we'll be given at least the same amount of time, and the witness made a prior statement, so I think that we will need some time for that too. So by the end of the week we'd appreciate it in the Pre-Trial Chamber would tell the Prosecution and -- well, all of us, what the plan is and when we're going to end in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... can tell us what the scheduling is for the next few days knowing that apparently next week what was scheduled will not materialise. I know that the Trial Chamber's legal officer invited the Prosecution to find witnesses for next week, and also I'm a bit vague as to the witnesses scheduled afterwards, prior to the 13th of December. Do you have any information, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, and good afternoon to Your Honours, counsel, and to everyone else. In respect of the scheduling that we envisioned for the remainder of this year, we distributed a calendar to counsel. I believe it was last week. It may have even been the week before, and I know there have been some changes. Unfortunately, mostly relating to witnesses who are not going to be coming as scheduled. However, Judge Ribicic is one that is still on our calendar as indicated for the 10th, I believe. I can also inform you, Mr. President, that in fact I spent most of this morning attempting to look into all possibilities of witnesses who might be able to come and to fill in some of the downtime for next week, those being witnesses identified by the Trial Chamber as potentially 92 bis witnesses who would need to come. I don't have any more information for Your Honours on that, and I -- I guess I would say that Mr. Scott yesterday said that he was not optimistic about next week, and I think to be candid, I would say that again today. We're not optimistic about next week, but we are attempting to recover. But certainly in respect of the forward schedule into December, we have every intention of bringing Judge Ribicic as scheduled, and so that will hold. And then on the 13th and the 12th, then, which would be the last two days prior to the break, I think that we still are holding those open in the hope that we'll be able to fill those again with perhaps one of the 92 bis witnesses that's been identified or suggested by the Trial Chamber. So that's -- that's the status at this moment. So Ribicic is on the calendar, and we're still looking to fill the additional time that remains in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, Judge Ribicic is scheduled on the 10th, isn't he? Couldn't he come next week? Because a judge is not overwhelmed with work, usually. So he might be able to come if he's advised of the need to come early enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We understand that he's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that I'm not speaking about myself when I speak about judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I understand that. I have every confidence that this Trial Chamber has plenty of work to do every day. I can inform you that Judge Ribicic is not in his home country of Slovenia, nor is he in Europe. He's out of Europe at a conference, and I can tell you for sure that he is not available next week, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, I can see that there are judges who have time enough to go and attend conferences, which unfortunately doesn't apply to me. Thank you for this information. We shall endeavour to do our best. Let's bring the witness in, and we hope we'll be able to complete his testimony today. It's absolutely necessary to finish him today. I understand that the first will be Mr. Ibrisimovic, since I've received his binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I hope everything works.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have the floor, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to say good afternoon to Mr. Masovic because we know each other from some other situations and we happen to be in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Ibrisimovic speak into his microphone. He's a long way away from his microphone and we can't hear him very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you put the microphone closer to your mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The first thing that I wanted to ask you, and you spoke about this yesterday, and I read this in an interview of yours perhaps a month or two ago that Bosnia-Herzegovina still has a lot of problems with the missing persons, and you even mentioned a figure of some 12.000 people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Perhaps the figure is a little smaller because some of those people have been found but not identified, so that their names are still on the list of missing persons or in fact they have been found but not identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: But it is a large number, a vast number, and that question, the question of missing persons and the large number, means that there are many grave sites that have not been discovered yet, I would say?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my experience, and I have had many years of experience, 15 years, in fact, we're still looking for 180 to 200 mass graves, graves with five or more victims in them, and probably several hundred other individual grave sites. Do you want me to repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I think it's been recorded. The second thing that I wanted to ask you, and I talked to Mr. Pusic about this, when I read your statement -- or statements, rather, I think there were three of them, and they related to what you know about Mr. Pusic and what I heard you say yesterday in court, was there a conflict of any kind between Mr. Pusic and you apart from the work you did in the commissions and so on?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We represented, during a period of time, two opposing sides. There were no personal conflicts, but we were on two different sides as negotiators, and after 1997, Mr. Pusic was chosen to be the first chief of the federal commission for missing persons, and I was appointed his deputy for the first three months, and then we continued to rotate, and one of us would be the chairman or vice-chairman of the federal commission. We would rotate until Mr. Pusic was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to hear that I was wrong in the impression I gained, because Mr. Pusic said your cooperation with him was mostly proper and correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of the negotiations that took place, I do believe that he tried to represent the interests of the party and the side that he represented, just as I tried to represent the interests of my side and the government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like now to go back to a question that was discussed yesterday that you testified, in fact, yesterday, the question of exhumations, and you said how you arrived at information, i.e., that you went on the site and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Excuse me, Mr. Ibrisimovic. You said something, Witness, and the counsel just glassed over it. It might be relevant. You said in 1997 Mr. Pusic was president of the federal commission and you yourself were his deputy, you said, and you added that he was dismissed. Why was he dismissed, and who did so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yesterday we touched upon that question, and I can confirm that in July 1997, by decision of the government of the federation Mr. Pusic was appointed the first presiding person, chairman, of the federal commission for missing persons, and I was appointed the vice-chairman. The decision had another provision which stated that the two of us would take turns in these two posts, the posts of chairman and vice-chairman, and that we would rotate every three months, and that's what happened. We took over from each other until Mr. Pusic was replaced, relieved of his duties in another commission which was called the commission for de-mining, which was at a state level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say both the Bosnian and Herzegovinian entities, but that decision about his replacement from the commission for de-mining automatically meant that he could no longer perform any other public offices in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that Mr. Pusic, to all intents and purposes, pursuant to that decision and being replaced in the commission for de-mining, he lost his post in the commission, the federal commission for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why? Why was he replaced? Was there a reason and, if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it was only Mr. Pusic who was replaced. I think the decision taken by the High Representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina comprised all three members of the commission for de-mining and that there was some talk of corruption, but I'm only telling you what I read in the media, not on the basis of any personal information that I had or any contacts with the gentleman. So all three members for the commission for de-mining were replaced from that post for reasons of corruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The decision was one in 2002, and it is true that they were all replaced. However, they were rehabilitated by 2004, and there were no legal proceedings taken against Mr. Pusic in the matter of corruption.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said what the media wrote about, what I read about in the papers and what I learnt through the media. That's what I said, how the media presented it, that they were replaced. Now, what happened later on, whether they were rehabilitated or not, I really don't know. Mr. Pusic did not return to the commission ever again, the commission for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to go back to a topic that you discussed with my learned friend yesterday, and that is the question of exhumation, and you've already described to us how the exhumations came about, in what way they were carried out. And we're going to use some documents now in that regard, so might the witness be provided with some documents. You told us yesterday that the number 16 was mentioned for the first time at the meeting that was held in Geneva, and as I understand it, it was an informal discussion between you and Mr. Pusic. It wasn't a formal meeting?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't it happened on the 20 of July during the excursion around Lake Geneva and to the town of Montreux.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Never before that or after that did Mr. Pusic mention this number, this number 16?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I took a look at your statements, you have them in front of you, but I don't think there's any need to look at them. When you gave a statement to the Prosecution, I don't think you mentioned the figure of 16. There was -- the figure of 12 and 13 and you explained that to us yesterday now would you take a look at the document, please, the first document. It's 6D 00758.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need some assistance here because I can't find my way in these numbers. Can you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: 6D 00758 is the number. And it's a document towards the end of the binder. That's where you'll find it. It is a letter, the main cantonal prosecutor's office in Mostar, Mr. Mehmed Basic. Mehmed Basic?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: He is informing -- yes, kindly make pauses between question and answer. Thank you. He is informing through the Federal Ministry of Justice in Sarajevo the Prosecution about what was done up until the 21st of September, 2007; right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is the report on exhumation, the photo -- photographs, photo documents, the DNA results, and then finally he says, "As for other information requested by the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY, please note that this prosecutor's office cannot provide you with that information at this moment because of the ongoing investigations in the matter," which mean the investigation had not been completed yet.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, we can go back to a document you saw led the number is P 100322. It's a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is a record on exhumation, and any exhumation is a very formal, very strict job which requires a procedure.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The people present were a prosecutor and an anthropologist of the international commission for missing.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Sanja Mulac on behalf of the commission for missing persons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The on-site investigation continued on the following day and the number is P 100323. That's the number of document, P 100323. On that day you were present as well?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose the reason was that you had received information that these could be the remains of the BiH army members and that's why you found yourself in Mostar on that day?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My colleagues from Republika Srpska who were there together with the prosecutor's office from Trebinje and started the exhumation, and Mrs. Mulac who was an observer observing the exhumation noticed some parts of uniforms, trousers and camouflage uniforms that the members of the BiH army wore during the conflict. That was the first time where a suspicion arose that those skeletons might belong to the Vranica building. However, at that moment on the 17 of May, we still didn't know that for a fact. On the 18th of May, and this document pertains to the 18th of May when I was there, on the 18th of May there were some very well-founded indicia that the bodies were of the prisoners from Vranica. On the arm of one of the victims we discovered a Seiko 50 watch with the date indicated on it as Thursday 14th. The on-site inspection revealed that Thursday the 14th was the month of May, 1993. Since this group was imprisoned on the 10th of May, this led us to assume that those people might hail from Vranica. However, at that moment we could not be certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: My questions were somewhat different. Mr. Mehmedic Nijaz, the Prosecutor was also present from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor from Trebinje was there?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The anthropologist of the international commission for missing persons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Karan, the pathologist from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the second page of this document the Prosecutor issues an order for these remains to be transferred to the city cemetery in Mostar where the laboratory findings will show how many bodies were located in the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and carry out the identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And here we have a sentence by the Prosecutor who says during the exhumation of skeletal remains of human origin it was very difficult to follow the continuity of the bodies because the skeletal remains were rather mixed up. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the last page of this document the forensic pathologist, Dr. Karan, says that this was a primary grave, and according to the exhumed remains, it could be concluded that the number of bodies was at least 20.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although this has been recorded in that way, at my question Dr. Karan told me that there were at least 24 different victims in that grave. And then I asked him how did he conclude that, because I had inspected the skeletal remains during the exhumation and I arrived at a conclusion that the figure was a bit lower. He told me that there were 24 right femurs, i.e., 24 upper leg bones. At that moment, I had my reservations about that, and on that same day when we took the remains over and when they were transported to the morgue in Stotina, we counted the bones of arms and legs, and we arrived at a conclusion that a maximum number of victims, judging by the number of the bones of the extremities, that there were no more than 16 victims altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: But I can't see it in the record.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not recorded on site. This is a record by our colleagues from Republika Srpska, i.e., the district prosecutor from Trebinje. The record on exhumation, as far as I know, was not drafted by the cantonal prosecutor from Mostar because the exhumation had been ordered and carried out by the prosecutor from Trebinje. As for the rest, the issue of the reassociation of the mortal remains from the 24 body bags that had been transported from the site, the question of the autopsy and final identification of the victims would be carried out pursuant to the order of the cantonal prosecutor in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecutor did not show you the findings on the anthropologist. This finding does not mention the number of 16 victims, does it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Eva Klanovska [as interpreted] doesn't say that the number of victims is 16.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What findings are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That is the findings of the institute -- or, rather, in international commission for missing persons which was signed by Dr. Eva Konovski -- Elvira Klanovska.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have it in my file?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you tell me the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: 10331 is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters are asking you to make breaks between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that this is not the final findings, that this is the preliminary findings based on the DNA analysis leading to the reassociation or matching of the body parts, but this findings does not mention the number of 16 bodies. The number 16 is not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This anthropological findings on reassociation does not show that the number of victims was 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You were -- you mentioned yesterday that the grave could even be a secondary grave.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm convinced that it was a secondary grave, because there were some parts of the skeletal remains missing. None of the 16 victims was complete. Each and every one of them is missing a part of the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that opinion. You have a lot of experience. I know that personally, but when it comes to such things and if we're talking about the secondary grave, then the reassociation and matching of the skeletal remains is very difficult, and it's very difficult to establish the exact number of victims.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, but the reassociation and the DNA analysis that have been carried out show clearly that some skeletal parts are missing, i.e., they were missing from the grave and they're missing in the morgue. For example, parts of the skull are missing. They're simply not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I was saying is that the procedure that has been carried so far points to the fact that there were 15 victims, and we don't have any official data confirming the number of 16.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have 15 names of the victims, and we have a 16th DNA analysis which does not match with the blood of any family that reported a missing relative. In the laboratory we have confirmation that there were 16 DNA samples that belonged to 16 different persons, 15 of which have been identified, and the 16th person has not been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we're talking about at cross-purposes. Anthropology is a very sophisticated science and requires a lot of knowledge, and this anthropological findings does not confirm that there were 16 bodies in that grave.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this findings, but if you're asking me as the head of the commission, what I know about this, I can confirm to you that we're talking about a total of 16 victims. Maybe it should be clarified why the reassociation is done in the first place. The reassociation is carried out in order to -- before the DNA analysis, in order to send as few skeletal samples as possible to the laboratory. In this particular case, instead of 16 samples that would have been normal to send if we had had 16 compact victims from a primary grave, for example, instead of sending 16 teeth from the 16 victims, we had to send 90 different specimen, 90 different samples. So if we're talking about 16 victims, on average it would be five or six samples per victim. This is what we did, because the skeletal remains were mixed up. The victims skulls had been fractured. The lower jaws had been separated from the upper part of the skull, and the anthropological analysis could not match the lower jaws with the bodies. If you are missing only two vertebrae in the spine, you -- you lose the continuity of the body and that's why you have to send for a DNA analysis two parts of the body, the upper part and the lower part. That's why the anthropological reassociation is done first, and the anthropologist, based on his expert knowledge, can determine which two legs belonged to one body. And then we don't send the samples from both those legs. We do not destroy the skeletal material. We usually send only one leg sample, usually the right leg sample. And when we obtain the DNA analysis from that leg then we know which leg is the left leg from the same body because anthropologically they are the same and the anthropology -- anthropologist can determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was suggesting to you that in such sensitive methods an error is something that happens. Let me give you an educational example. A gentleman whom we know, a professor who died, when the grave was opened he determined that there were five skeletal remains, and later on it was determined that there were actually six bodies in question.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a good example. I'm glad you mentioned it. Dr. Klanovska during the exhumation established that there were six victims in question which the local forensic expert, unfortunately, did not accept, and later on through DNA analysis it was confirmed that the number was actually six.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel come closer to the microphone and would the counsel and would the witness and counsel please note overlap.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you said it, he was a pathologist, a forensic pathologist. The reassociation is not an issue for forensic pathologists but for forensic anthropologists. Those are the persons that share the same qualifications with Dr. Klanovska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is when grave is opened, especially if the secondary grave is in question, an error is not excluded.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a secondary grave is opened, the experts may make a mistake, and I said it in the introduction to my testimony. Dr. Karan who was in charge of this exhumation said and you can see it in the record, he said 20 bodies at least. To me he said 24 bodies, Dr. Klanovska and the DNA confirmed that the number was actually 16. There were 16 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: We have agreed that that number does not figure in Dr. Klanovska's findings, so we can move on to another topic. The talks between you and Mr. Pusic about Vranica, I know that Vranica was something that was something that -- for which there was a lot of pressure, but there were some other issues, Bugojno, and other things, that also burdened your relationship.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that our relationship was burdened but not so much our relationship but the negotiations because of the complexity of the matter, because of the interdependence of these cases and the whole situation resulted in a stalemate, and even those things that could have been solved because of the circumstances and the sensitivity of these cases, and yesterday I spoke about the case -- cases of Vranica and Bugojno, two very similar cases on two different sides. In the Vranica case this was aired on TV, and in the Bugojno case the victims were registered by the International Red Cross, and they had sent messages to their families that they were alive, that they were healthy, and after that these people were taken away and probably killed, because they have been missing for 14 years now. There are some testimonies about their killings and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that there was a lot of pressure both on you and Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- this was one of the cases of the many cases that for a number of years --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I ask Mr. Ibrisimovic and also you, Witness, that you have to really make some pause and break between your questions and answers. It was also asked by the president a few minutes ago, and it is our constant problem, and not only ours but mainly the interpreters, that especially when you are speaking your mother tongue, then of course you are not going to take care of the speed of your talking, and please do so, and be so kind to really helping the interpreters in this way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll do our best to make everybody's work easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and follow the screen, the display on the screen, and then wait until I see it appearing on the screen and then give my answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat a question, because I don't think the answer was recorded. I asked you before Geneva and after Geneva, when you talked to Mr. Pusic about Vranica, the number 16 was never mentioned. It was always 12 or 13 for missing persons; is that right? You told me that that was so; right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Mostly the figures mentioned were 13 people from Vranica, that is before Geneva and after Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at your file then you'll find document 2 -- 6D 00749. If you look at page 3, you'll see it's a letter from Mr. Pusic requesting from the security services of Mostar to provide him with information with respect to the fate of the persons missing, both Croats and Bosniaks, who went missing during the conflict. And the date is the 3rd of August, 1995. So that's towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two documents under that same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's a three-page document, and if you look at the third page.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a different date on the third page. It says the 28th of July, 1995, and they're different documents in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The date here is the 28th of July, 1995, where Mr. Pusic is writing to the SIS in Mostar, and the date, the 3rd of August, is the reply to the request made by Mr. Pusic with respect to the missing soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The answer refers to Mr. Pusic's letter.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that something's missing here, that I'm missing the first page of this document, because these three pieces of paper are quite obviously not the total document in the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take it in chronological order. Let's look at the first document dated the 28th of July, 1995. Let's look at that first.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is a letter from Mr. Pusic to the Mostar security service; right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when we have that, then we have a letter from the security and information service of Mostar of the 3rd of August, which refers to the letter sent by Mr. Pusic. All I want to say is that Mr. Pusic raised this issue, the issue of the missing soldiers, after the conflicts which were over in 1994. So the question of the soldiers missing from Vranica, and Mr. Pusic wrote about this, that was 10 or 11 years ago, of course, and he asked for more information.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say explicitly here that they are searching for members of the army from Vranica. That's the first point. Secondly, in my opinion this document doesn't follow any logic. If Mr. Pusic, in July 1995, speaks about an exchange of the bodies of those who were killed, then there's something amiss there, something that's not in order, because in Washington we reached an agreement to release all the prisoners and to hand over the bodies of those people who had been killed, and from mid-1994 or thereabouts there were no more exchanges of dead bodies between the BH army and the HVO, Croatian Defence Council. So I don't know why in July 1995 he would be referring to exchanges, because at that time the exchange of either living persons or dead persons just took place between the BH army and the Serb side, and the Croatian Defence Council and the Serb side. But there was no mutual exchange as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it wasn't put in the best way, but what I want to say is that he did raise the issue, and he requested information about missing persons, and at that time members from the -- the army members from the Vranica building were considered missing.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. They were considered missing until the 18th of May or a little after the 18th of May when the first DNA results arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go back to something you were talking about yesterday. The Presiding Judge asked you a question. I know that in August 1992 you became a member of the commission, and it was called the State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War at the time. Now, would you have a look at 6D 00798, please. That's another document in your file.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I have is 00757. That's the last document in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: 6D 708. I'm sorry, I made a mistake. I meant to say 708. That's the last number. The president of the commission was the Deputy Justice Minister, Mr. Bibic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, but there's a mistake in the translation. It says Bibic. It should be Muhibic. That's the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In Article 7 of this decision on the establishment of the commission the mandate of the commission is set out, its terms of reference. And you testified about that yesterday, did you not?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next document, P 3191. P 3191. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is a decision dated the 5th of July, 1993, where Mr. Pusic is being appointed the head of the service for the exchange of prisoners and other persons, and under that we have the decision on the establishment of the service, and in Article 2 its mandate, the is service's mandate. And if you compare the mandate of the state commission from the BH government decision and Article 2 of this decision, then that mandate is more or less the same, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the mandate of the state commission was a little broader in scope. So the state commission for the exchange of prisoners of war and persons deprived of liberty, records of those killed, wounded, and missing. That's the additional mandate which is broader and is set out in the title. It is a broader mandate than this decision that you're pointing to. And the state commission in, its composition, had three subcommissions. One was for the exchange of POWs. One was for records of those missing, and a third one was for the records of those dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to show you that the HVO had a similar department or service dealing with these questions. Now, which had broader authority doesn't matter. I just wanted to show that this service existed and that it dealt with those matters. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the proviso that the state commission was established in April, the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is a July 1992 decision. Perhaps it was established earlier or taken earlier, but it was published in July 1992. The state commission on the basis of this was formed in July 1992. The decision was made public in the Official Gazette. It might have been actually established earlier on, but the prime minister signed the decision in 1992 and that's when it was made public. And you became a member in August 1992, did you not?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, but within the Ministry of Defence I think the then minister of defence, which was Mr. Jerko Doko, already in April had established a commission for exchanges, which was functioning in April. And then at the level of the BH government a decision was taken in July to establish a state commission with the full title that it had and that we mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you met Mr. Pusic for the first time on the 29th of December, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I contacted another member, had contacts with another member, or, rather, Mr. Pusic's deputy, and that was on the 9th of November, 1993, in Jablanica and Konjic where we reached an agreement to release persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had information that the exchange took place at a local level and that it functioned fairly well, that there was no need for you to intervene.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two reasons for which I did not intervene. One was that the exchanges functioned to all intents and purposes not only at the level of Herzegovina but Vitez, Travnik, Busovaca, Kiseljak. That is to say -- and Zenica in Central Bosnia, that is, and the other reason, as I said, was about the blockades, that Sarajevo was under siege three -- for three and a half years, and after the conflict broke out between the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council there was a blockade and siege of Mostar as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So you received reports from time to time, but there were no problems, no major problems with respect to the exchanges between the HVO and these local commissions?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's right. But I'd like to say that they were exchanges of a lesser intensity and -- involving fewer people. So lower-level exchanges. Mostly they were a number of wounded from both sides, members of the two sides' armies, or the exchange of bodies of people who had been killed in combat, and also in part POW exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you say -- in your statement I came across a section where you said that Dziho Orucevic, Juso Jeli [as interpreted] were involved in all that, Dziho, Zlatan Buljko, et cetera. People who dealt with this, were involved in this during that period would be better placed to talk about it, and those people who negotiated with Mr. Pusic during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of Mr. Zlatan Buljko. I don't think I know him, judging by his first and last name. And even if he did attend some of the negotiations that I attended, it might have been just once. But as I say, the name does not sound familiar. And apart from the other people you mentioned, I remember Mr. Ali Alikadic when it comes to Herzegovina, and in the case of Central Bosnia I -- on the BH army side, the negotiations were conducted by Samir Sefer from Travnik, and Mrs. Bolic, Emira Bolic [phoen] from Zenica, as well as Mr. Causevic, Spaho Causevic, the head of the district commission for the exchange of POWs for Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned Mr. Buljko's name because he testified here, and he said that he attended some negotiations with Mr. Pusic, but it doesn't matter. We won't go into that if you say you don't know him. Now, the relationship between the state commission and the other commissions that existed on the ground, the army commissions, was there a relationship of subordination? Was one -- were some superior, others subordinate? Were they duty-bound to report back and, if so, to whom? Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two periods in the development of the state commission, two stages. After the formation of the district as a -- or districts as administrative units in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm not sure when that was, the regional commissions were formed in Tuzla, Mostar, Bihac, and in Zenica, too, and those regional commissions were responsible to the state commission -- or, rather, to the president of the state commission, and they had the duty when negotiating with the opposing side or sides that if they reached an agreement for an exchange of some kind they would have to request permission from the president of the state commission, who would then approve it or not, but mostly he approved it. There were just situations that were challenged when -- if they were -- if -- if they concerned persons who were in prison under the government's control and against whom legal proceedings had been initiated. So those persons were not included in the exchange process before the Presidency as the head of state made the decision to pardon them if they had been found guilty or unless an amnesty was decided. I think in March 1993, attached to the corps of the BH army commissions were established to take care of the prisoners of war, and for a time those acted autonomously, independently. And let me tell you that we for a time had some disagreements with those commissions, because they did not respect the requests of the state commission for exchanging prisoners of war. Later on in the contacts we had, that is to say the state commissions relationships and contacts with the Ministry of Defence and with the General Staff of the BH army, an agreement was reached whereby those commissions, too, were duty-bound to act pursuant to the state commission's instructions for the exchange of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment those military commission were not under the umbrella of the government commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were never formally part of the state commission. They were part of the respective corps of the BiH army, and they were led by the military personnel, and they were responsible to the corps commanders. I'm talking about the commissions that took care of the POWs that were established as of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: But I believe these commissions had a mandate to somehow participate in the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They joined us. Their representatives would later on be sent to the negotiations and they were present at all the negotiations where I was and where negotiations were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I found it in some reports that your counterpart in Central Bosnia was Nikica Petrovic; is that correct? I'm talking about Vitez and Srednja Bosna [as interpreted] and in Kiseljak it was Mr. Ivo Miro Jovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Until recently he was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, the correct name is Ivo Miro Jovic. And the area is Kiseljak. This has not been recorded. Yesterday you testified under oath and you spoke about those meetings and negotiations with Mr. Pusic. I assume, I was never a negotiator in such a situation, when you come for negotiations you have a programme you have a mandate you have a goal that you want to achieve; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Every negotiator by the logic of things want -- wants to achieve a maximum, to get as much as they can out of those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: However, the negotiations were not only in the domain of Mr. Masovic and Mr. Pusic. Things would sometimes be resolved at levels higher than you. You had to follow somebody's instructions. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say above us?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes things would happen that you did not have any influence on. You could not influence them, either you or Mr. Pusic, when it came to your negotiations.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please could you more precise? What exactly do you have in mind when you ask me that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and do that. When it comes to negotiations, this would be preceded by political negotiations at a high political level or a military level. Mr. Masovic and Mr. Pusic were there to implement things that had been agreed on prior to your negotiations. Wouldn't that be correct? You mentioned the occasion when Mr. Silajdzic came to Konjic and Jablanica. Mr. Komsic, a member of the Presidency, said it was a high -- a delegation at a very high level.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us say that there were two periods, the period leading up to the Washington Agreement, i.e., the period leading up to the political negotiations which would result in the Washington Agreement. During that period of time, the commissions for exchanges worked in keeping with their mandates without any political influences or interference. Once the bilateral decision was reached on the matters between the army and the HVO to be normalised, from then on all negotiations, including the negotiations on POWs would take place at a political level, which was the highest political level, which included the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., the head of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic, the president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman, and later on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Silajdzic and Granic respectively, and Mr. Pusic and myself were only duty bound with the assistance of the International Committee of the Red Cross and other international organisations that were involved in the program of missing persons to carry out the political agreements and implement them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I was saying. If the Washington Agreement was signed and it was and we all know who signed it, neither Mr. Masovic nor Mr. Pusic could have any say in the implementation of this agreement. It would have been carried out with or without you. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing is certain. In order to implement the Washington Sporzum with respect to the missing persons and prisoners of war, it would have been carried out with or without -- without the two of us. The two of us could have a say in the speed with which that agreement was carried out, and we did have influence on that. When it comes to Mr. Pusic, I must say that this influence was negative, unfortunately. In the implementation of the agreement, some things were -- were taking a lot of time, much too longer than necessary when this came to the liberation of prisoners. This took place only two months after the signing of the Washington Agreement. The last prisoners were released in the second half of April, i.e., one number of prisoners were kept even after that. There were even some new arrests even after the Washington Agreement was signed. Some prisoners, i.e., some detainees, since there were no more fighting between the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, some people were arrested when they were trying to do some shopping in Kiseljak, and then after the Washington Agreement, they were also subject of our negotiations. I must say that at one point in time, and that was on the 12th of April or maybe the 13th of April, 1994, because of the problems of missing, i.e., because of the problems of prisoners, the Washington Agreement was at a stake at that time, namely Mr. Pusic refused to release all prisoners as had been agreed as per Washington Agreement, and at that moment the President of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman, sent to Medjugorje his representative for humanitarian issues, Mr. Slobodan Lang, who had a mission to humour Mr. Pusic and make him agree to the final release of all prisoners. I witnessed of some very hard talks between Mr. Lang and Mr. Pusic. At that point Mr. Lang was even speaking about a possible removal from Mr. Pusic -- of Mr. Pusic from the position because of his refusal to implement the agreement and release all the prisoners. At that point, I proposed a compromise, which was later on translated into a written agreement between the two of us, and finally that agreement was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In any case that part of the Washington Agreement was implemented?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with minor delays, but if you look at that situation from the perspective of a person who had spent months in camps and in prison, then the delay would be rather long. In Heliodrom, for example, in the Heliodrom camp, the detainees put up a strike about the time when Mr. Lang arrived. I know that Mr. Lang visited the prisoners. They were on a hunger strike, and he tried to persuade them to call off the hunger strike, because some sort of agreement on their release would eventually be achieved. He even said that if the detainees continued with their hunger strike that the HVO had a possibility to start force-feeding them in keeping with the provisions on, I think, the Tokyo declaration. I believe that the Tokyo declaration came into play, and according to that declaration from the moment when the detainees could no longer think rationally and when their health is at stake those who kept them detained had every right to start force-feeding them by giving them infusions and this could be done against their own will.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lang did come to Mostar but not because of Mr. Pusic, but because Mr. Tudjman was one of the signatories of the agreement together with Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Silajdzic, and Mr. Granic. And I'm putting it to you that Mr. Tudjman probably had never heard of Mr. Pusic, but let's leave that aside for the time being. Can we now look at another document, which is P 7851. This is a report by Mr. Pusic. Did you find it, Mr. Masovic?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your name is mentioned in here. This is a report on a meeting that took place on the 12th of January, 1994, and you can see a short report about the negotiations, and it says that within the shortest possible time all the prisoners should be released according to the all-for-all principle.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I give you an answer, it says here 12th of January, and you said 12th February, which is correct. 12th February is correct. The document bears a very strange date, as if it had been drafted on the 12th of January, 1994, a month prior to the negotiations. I suppose this is a typo in the document. I can confirm that the meeting took place on the 12th of February, 1994, and the participants were Mr. Pusic and myself, and this took place on the premises of the Spanish Battalion in Medjugorje. And I can also confirm that what it says here in the report reflects the totality of the essence of what we had agreed, with the exception of the last paragraph in which Mr. Pusic, in his report, says that we would meet again in Jablanica on the 17th of February, 1994, where we were to continue negotiations with respect to Bugojno and other detention facilities. I can only assume why Mr. Pusic added that last paragraph. I suppose this had to do with the possible pressure on the part of the Croatian families in Bugojno because of the answer to the destiny of the 21 prisoners who had been arrested in Bugojno. In other words, the last paragraph was never discussed on the 12th of February, and this is not what we agreed, and this is not what is indicated in the official statement that was signed by myself and Mr. Pusic after the meeting and sent as a statement for the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then look at this public statement, which is 6D 00499.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that this is the draft. The handwriting is mine. This is the public statement which I drafted. And if you read --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So you have agreed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will see that there's no mention of Bugojno as part of our agreement, just as I have explained answering your previous question. As for the rest, the report of Mr. Pusic about the negotiations corresponds to my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just make a distinction. Mr. Pusic's report is what he drafted, and this here is your joint statement, and here we also have an indication that in the shortest possible time -- possible time everybody will be released -- released according to the all-for-all principle.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first paragraphs in Mr. Pusic's report are the reflection of what had been agreed. The thing that is not correct and does not reflect what we had agreed is that we agreed to meet on the 17th of February to discuss the issue of Bugojno and other prisons, and that's why I have not included that into my statement for the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the following document which is P 7861. This is an UNPROFOR report, the civilian affairs of the UNPROFOR report.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is page 5 in the translation. You can look at page 6. And the title is "Negotiations about the release of prisoners of war." It will be the penultimate page in the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whilst he's looking, Mr. Ibrisimovic, you've already used up one hour and five minutes. So you are five minutes past your time. Are there other Defence teams that gave away some of their time to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Petkovic's Defence has ceded its time to me, but I will complete my examination within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the document before me. My name -- or, rather, my surname has been written wrongly on the document, but quite obviously it does refer to the meeting that we talked about on the 12th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And you agreed for an all-for-all exchange and that the ICRC would be involved.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next document. P 8093 is the number. It is the report by the monitoring mission of the European Community, and you can take a look at page 4. And the title of the section is "Humanitarian issues." The document is dated the 19th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your name is mentioned as well as Mr. Pusic's name, and the observers or monitors note that everything is going well, that what was agreed is being implemented; right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have here, if I can put it, a jump. What Mr. Pusic and I agreed on the 12th of February, 1994, in Medjugorje was in part implemented on the 1st of March, 2004. So on that day, the BH army released 61 members of the Croatian Defence Council, and the Croatian Defence Council, for its part, released 121 prisoners from Heliodrom. And I think that mostly they were Bosniaks from the village of Sovici. I think it belongs to Jablanica municipality, that village. So that was how the agreement was put into effect, the agreement of the 12th of February, 2004. Now, what is mentioned in this document here, which I have before me, is in fact the implementation of another agreement between Mr. Pusic and myself, which was reached in Gornji Vakuf in 19 -- on the 17th of March, 2004. And pursuant to that agreement, we took it upon ourselves to release a certain number of prisoners from both sides. And the agreement, to the best of my recollections, was implemented fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That's the agreement you discussed with my learned friend yesterday. That's why I didn't mention it. But it was P 08084, the 17th of March agreement, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to that agreement, the HVO freed about 19 -- well, around the 19th and 20th or 22nd of March about 750 prisoners from Heliodrom and the military remand prison at Ljubuski. The BH army freed that group of 73 members of the HVO and HV from Mostar, and it also freed 294 members of the Croatian Defence Council from Bugojno. And on the 22nd of March, it freed six members of the Croatian Defence Council from Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned this group of 121 persons who were released pursuant to this agreement. Now, would you look at document P 7985 now, please. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see here that the military prosecutor's office of Mostar is writing to the service for the exchange of captured and other persons, that is to say to Mr. Pusic, the military prosecutor Mladen Jurisic. I believe you know Mr. Jurisic, do you not? He was the president of the court in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know Mr. Jurisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: He says, and he's referring to Mr. Pusic's letter, that the military prosecutor's office approves the agreed-upon exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two comments to make regarding this document. The first is this: Allegedly these people were suspects. They were suspected of having belonged to the enemy army. And so this -- they were suspect pursuant to Article 119, para 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I know what you want to say, but let me stop you. My question was different. This is the procedure that Mr. Pusic had to respect, that is to say the -- when the military prosecutor gives a green light for people to be exchanged he would have to act upon it, regardless of whether legal proceedings are were being conducted or not. That was my question. So is that what follows from this document? Is that what this document shows?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prosecutor, Mr. Jurisic, did not have the legal authority, authority under the law, to release for and send for exchange any individual who was being militarily -- who was being legally prosecuted. There was no law to state he could, either in the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina or in the laws enacted by the then-Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Nowhere does it say -- is there a provision whereby a military prosecutor can pardon or amnesty somebody against whom legal proceedings have been taken. He could not prosecute them and place the prisoners at the disposal of Mr. Pusic or the service for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let us leave that to others whether regulations existed or not, provisions and laws existed or not, but Mr. Pusic had to respect what the military prosecutor told him to do. That was the procedure, was it not?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't agree with you on that point. Mr. Pusic did not have to seek this approval. He should have sought approval from the organ in charge of pardoning these prisoners, abolishing their sentence, and then to free them through the exchange process, not to release them for an exchange process, whereas, as it says here, the military prosecutor's office is legally prosecuting them. So that would mean that you're going to be released, but the lawsuit against you is still in force. You won't find anything like that in any of the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was the position of the military prosecutor's office, but Mr. Pusic couldn't influence that in any way. But anyway, we're talking about not the exchange of 121 persons. That was implemented fully as you had agreed; right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's quarter to 4.00. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic, according to our calculations, you have 11 minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like Mr. Masovic now to take a look at just a couple of more documents. One of them is 6D 00580. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is a document coming from the cabinet of the offices of the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Selim Novalic personally. You know him, do you?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It says here the president considers that the exchange should take place on the principle of one for one, that is say that the same number of Bosnian prisoners as members of the HVO should be released. And now we have here that the BH army or, rather, the government and the Presidency are insisting on the principle of one or one and not all for all.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this document I cannot confirm the authenticity of it. It's not logical, as far as I can see, in the sense that they are jumping over me as the head of the commission, and somebody subordinate to me is discussing this directly with the cabinet and the Presidency. And in any case, this isn't Mr. Izetbegovic's signature. I don't see on the document any number, protocol number, reference number, anything like that. However -- well, this is the first time that I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't the president who signed it. It says the cabinet of the president. I think that this is the signature of Alija Selimovic, Chef de Cabinet, but we obtained this document from the Prosecution. So the authenticity of the document cannot be challenged.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to go into that. I'm not authorised to do so, to test the authenticity of the document or whatever. All I can notice is that there's no protocol number and that it is not Mr. Izetbegovic's signature there, because I know his signature, because during the war and after the war, through the various documents on pardons signed by him I was able to see his signature and recognise the documents. But if it is indeed an authentic document and if it is an offer for the exchange of 227 HVO members for 39 members of the BH army and a 10-member Tuzla delegation, then what I can tell you is that this exchange was implemented in a quite a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you but what I'm saying is that's what the principle was at that point in time and if you look on the left-hand side you can see that this was sent by Paket link, Paket communication. If you can recognise that on the original document at 1525 hours on the 26th of September, 1993. That's when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I state that that wasn't the principle at any time, that time or any other time, and this was borne out by practice later on including what happened in this specific case. And in this specific case what happened was the following: The Croatian Defence Council freed 500 prisoners from Gabela camp. It also released 39 members of the BH army from Konjic, and it freed not a ten-member but a nine-member Tuzla delegation, that is to say, a delegation of civilians travelling to Split on a humanitarian aid mission. And in that delegation there was the mufti, Husein Efendi Kavazovic that I referred to yesterday, and in addition to him in the delegation there was also Mr. Alija Muminovic, later on the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Jordan. And on our side, the BH army side on this occasion, it wasn't 227 members of the Croatian Defence Council who were released but 309 HVO members were released from the prison in Konjic. And on the side of the HVO at the same time, a Frenchman was freed. I am not sure what his status was, whether he was a journalist or a humanitarian aid worker or something else, but I do know that he was incorporated in this exchange agreement and that on our side we asked that that man be freed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: We can look at the next document, 6D 00762. 6D 00762. It is a document of the Supreme Command Staff of the armed forces, dated the 25th of August, 1993. And the commander -- for the commander Stjepan Siber, and he says in point 1 exchange prisoners of war in the following manner and procedure, namely exchange one for one. 150 for 150 persons. Oh, in the ratio of 1:1. And the Tuzla delegation is mentioned there as well.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Here, too, we see that at that point in time the leaders of the army advocated the one-for-one principle.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document -- or, rather, the second document shows that this is the same exchange. The Tuzla delegation that was never carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You've already spoken about that. I just wanted to point to bullet point 1, and you have explained that. Yesterday you were shown the alleged interview with Mr. Pusic in "Slobodna Dalmacija". Just for the record, this is P 90 -- P 949. I have my reservations about any sort of interview and Mr. Pusic told me that he does not remember either the journalist or the interview, and I know that you have had some negative experiences with the press. A lot has been written about you as well. And some wrong information was published that did not reflect your position. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you give me some examples, I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Somebody called Mitrovic said that -- or wrote that you know what happened at Ozren, and a pamphlet was also published in which your name was mentioned, and I also read some of your statements here at the Tribunal for which, I believe, they are distorted. What I'm saying is that sometimes the press does not really carry the opinion that people uphold.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're talking about. These were not my statements. Those were the statements by other people. As far as I know, I don't have that kind of experience. At least I can't remember any at this moment. I cannot remember anybody distorting my information in the media. Maybe some statements were curtailed because the media never give you enough space. I have so much to say and I'm never given enough space. But I don't remember anybody misinterpreting a statement of mine. I really do not have any influence on what other people say about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I read you. Of course you mentioned in your statement that Mr. Ivica Zelic that you knew about the whereabouts of the victims or remains that went missing from Ozren; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: But you refuted that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I did or not but I suppose I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I talked with Mr. Pusic about Vranica not only about Vranica but also about Bugojno, and Mr. Pusic told me that the same person, Ivica Zelic, i.e., some other people, said that you knew what happened to the people in Bugojno and Mr. Pusic said that this was speculation because you certainly don't know what happened to these people. And this is a pure speculation, and you know nothing about that, and that if you did know then that information would be available to everybody.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I have known for quite a while what happened to these people. After having been taken out from the prison, those people were obviously liquidated. If they hadn't, I'm sure that one of them at least would rejoin their families within the 14 years. What I know [as interpreted] until this very moment is where their mortal remains were buried, and this is one part of my mandate within the federal commission for missing persons and within the institute for missing persons. I also don't know the whereabouts of the 13.000 other people that went missing during the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly what I meant when I said that Mr. Pusic said that this is speculation that you know where these people who have probably been killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, and witness, I just want to make sure the transcript is correct, or correctly reflects the witness's answer in respect of his knowledge of the Bugojno group because what we're seeing in English at line 9 is what he says is "what I know" -- "what I know, until this very moment is where their mortal remains were buried," and I -- it was my understanding based on the witness's testimony yesterday that perhaps he means to say something else, but I just want to make sure the record clearly reflects his knowledge on that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. That's not what I said. I said that I am aware of their destiny, and I also said that what I don't know is where they were buried. That's what I don't know. Although, this is part of my mandate to learn, amongst other things, where their mortal remains, the mortal remains of the 21 prisoners were buried. We can say with a high degree of certainty that they were killed. If they hadn't been killed, they would turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that I wanted to hear from you. Mr. Pusic told me that it would be a spear speculation to tell -- to say that you know where these people are buried. And somebody else said that, and said that to him, and he claims that this is simply not the truth. You don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I knew where they were buried, you would not have to ask me that, because as soon as I learnt I would have undertaken the steps that are within my purview. I would have undertaken exhumation through the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that you don't know, that this is pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I'm saying in confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I also believe that stories like that are pure speculation. You don't know, and I have no further questions, and I would like to thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next counsel, please. For 30 minutes. You have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Masovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I begin my cross-examination I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that I have one hour at my disposal, 30 minutes that we have anyway, and 30 minutes that we were given by the Prlic Defence. And I'll try and complete my cross-examination even before the time allocated to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, in your testimony you have spoken about the position of the government in Sarajevo and that was said yesterday that people can be exchanged only if they are considered prisoners of war or civilians against whom legal proceedings were conducted for crimes in relation to the armed conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but I would like to -- that against whom proceedings are conducted or are still underway, because the exchange also comprised those for whom the conviction had not been passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll try and make the appropriate breaks before I'm warned to help the interpreters and to have everything recorded. So according to you the policies of the government in Sarajevo was not to evacuate the civilians from the territory under the control of the HVO. The evacuation of Bosnian civilians, that is, from the territory under the control of the HVO, or the evacuation of Croats to other territories from the territories where they were residing at that moment.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The policy in place was not to evacuate the civilians. Yesterday I started talking about that, but I did not complete my testimony. I said that the High Commissioner for Refugees at certain moments put a lot of pressure on the government in Sarajevo to allow the evacuation of certain groups of civilians which in the view of the UNHCR were under particular threat.
