I personally spoke to some members of the Presidency about that problem because a moral dilemma arose with that respect whether to include such civilians into some sort of exchanges that the Serb side insisted on and later on Mr. Pusic joined them. If we are done that, we would have gotten involved in the process of ethnic cleansing that the government in Sarajevo was against throughout all this time. I'm talking about the policies, but I may be able to anticipate your next question, and I can tell you that it did happen that the government or the local authorities did get involved in this type of evacuation of civilians, but mostly those civilians that were threatened, whose life or health were endangered in some centres or whatever you want to call them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I have only one hour, and sometimes I will have to stop your answers, because I just don't have the time for any longer elaborations. I remember you having said that yesterday, and that information is very precious to us when you say that they participated in UNHCR, that is. Yesterday you spoke about the exchange in November that you assisted in Konjic during which 550 Bosniaks were exchanged and the Tuzla mufti Kavazovic was in that group. That was in November, in early November 1993 or thereabouts; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exchange took place on the 19th of October, 1993. Five hundred prisoners from Gabela --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You've already told us that. No need to go over that again. Do you know, tell us, where had that group been? I'm talking about the group of civilians, Bosniaks. Where had they been kept physically?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had been detained in a house. I was in that location on that day, on the 19th of October, together with Mr. Silajdzic. The name of the place was either Turija or Zabrdje. Those were two places where prisoners were kept. There was a house there where they were kept, and on that day I even talked to some of them, because a number of them had been taken from the prison and handed over to the Serb side. One of them actually never reappeared alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now you have provided me with the information that I was interested in, and that is that on the 19th of October, on that visit Mr. Silajdzic was with you.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Silajdzic, there was also Mr. Komsic, Father Andjelovic and in the prison, i.e., at the place of the exchange, there was Mr. Silajdzic, myself, Mr. Silajdzic's bodyguard and Mr. Selim Novalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that when we're talking about this exchange Mr. Silajdzic had proposed to the HVO unit in Turija to evacuate from the area the HVO and Croatian civilians in exchange of money?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look in my binder, the first document in my binder, and the number is P 06555. I apologise, I thought that everybody had the documents already. The document is P 06555. It's the first in the binder. Tell me when you've got it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now can now look at it together look at the signatory of this document. That's Mladen Zovko, also known as Kuhar. Did you ever have contact with him?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This is the man who was our counterpart in Konjic with whom we discussed the exchange that was implemented on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the first sentence of this document by the Herceg Stjepan Turija Independent Battalion it says that during talks with Haris Silajdzic for whom you confirmed that he was in Turija on that day, that there was -- there were talks with him regarding the exchange of prisoners of war. In addition to the Independent Battalion, the meeting was attended by Jerko Petrovic, and in addition to Silajdzic on the Muslim side there was also Salko Music, the commander of the 6th Corps, and a member of the Supreme Commander Bosiocic, also known as Zagi. The second paragraph is very significant. "In addition to the talks about the exchange, the aforementioned individuals offered us to surrender our positions to them and in exchange they would enable the evacuation of soldiers and civilians from our free territories across their territory." It says further on: "During the talks Haris Silajdzic undertook to personally provide guarantees regarding possible -- a possible operation." The document continues by saying that on the 3rd of November, 1993, the signatory of this document, Mr. Mladen Zovko had a conversation with Fahrudin Fazlic, also known as Braco, who informed him that he had been authorised by Silajdzic to continue negotiations and he goes on to say, "On that occasion he offered to buy from us 70 per cent of small arms, all the heavy weapons and food that has remained and they were prepared to pay for that 500.000 German marks." The document goes on to say and I would like to emphasise a detail in this document that: "On the 5th of November I met with Fazlic again and on that occasion I was informed that as a guarantee we should be escorted by the commander of the 6th Corps and Haris Silajdzic." This letter was sent by this commander to Mostar to Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, Lucic, and asks them what to do with regard to the offer that he has received. Do you know anything about that? It transpires clearly from this document that in exchange for the evacuation of the HVO and civilians from the territory money has been offered and that the political leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina is involved in that. Are you familiar with this development? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. As you can see, my name is not mentioned here. I was not present in any such thing. I was with Mr. Silajdzic throughout the exchange. I told you that we were together in Konjic on the premises of the 6th Corps. Mr. Zovko came there as well. Later on I was in the same APC with Mr. Silajdzic as we went for the exchange, and we returned together to Sarajevo. I -- I don't know whether I'm authorised to comment upon a document of this kind that I don't know anything about that. Even if there had been such a conversation, I did not attend it. But it doesn't make sense. The HVO was in a more powerful position, and the BiH army was not in a position to offer them anything in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what was the position of that part of the HVO in Turija? Do you know what was their position at that time, and do you know why the Tuzla delegation had been captured in the first place? Do you know that they were encircled at the time, that on the one hand they had been expelled from Konjic, that the BH army was on one side, and on the other side there was the Serb army, and that in that so-called Konjic pocket that has been discussed on so many occasions in this -- in this courtroom that they were encircled and that out of sheer desperation that they had captured the delegation in order to draw some attention to themselves? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I know that there was certain co-operation and I've already spoken about that. I started talking about that because the captives that the HVO had captured who were members of the BiH army had been handed over to the Serb side for investigation and interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And one of them was killed. His name was Rasim Makan.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And a large number of HVO members were also killed in that area, too, but I was just asking you about this document. You said you don't know anything about it, that you can't comment on it, and that you weren't present. Now, my colleague asked you about the relationship of the political leaders towards the exchanges, and he showed you a moment ago two documents, and for the transcript they were 6D 00580, and 6D 00762. Now, from these two documents we saw the position of the Presidency, or cabinet, President's cabinet, the president of the BH republic, of course, and the top army leaders including Mr. Siber. Linked to this exchange they suggest an exchange on the one-to-one principle. I know, Mr. Masovic, that you said that that exchange did not take place in that way but I'm going to show you a document now and the number of that document is 2D 00590 and it is the last document in my binder but unfortunately actually it's not in my binder. It's an additional document attached to the binder. We have on it e-court luckily. Just tell me when you've found it, please.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We can see here this is a document from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Konjic municipality. It is a decision dated the 1st of October, 1993, and I'm just going to remind you that in the document that was shown to you by my colleague Mr. Ibrisimovic a moment ago, and it is the letter from the cabinet of the president, it says that the letter was sent by Paket communication to Konjic and here it says the War Presidency of Konjic municipality at a meeting held on the 1st of October, 1993, is issuing the following decision, and it is signed by Mr. Cibo. Does the name ring a bell? Is it familiar? Mr. Safet Cibo.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Mr. Cibo was for a time the president of the wartime Presidency of Konjic municipality, Jablanica, too, and I think Prozor. Three municipalities, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Fine. It was a conjoining of municipalities just for wartime conditions outside constitutional principles, and he was the president of those three municipalities; right? Can we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the reasons why these municipalities were joined up and why he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. But pursuant to the constitution, you and I are both lawyers and we know that, that according to the BH constitution they -- there was no community of municipalities. It's just that Mr. Cibo was given authority to be the president of those three municipalities at that time.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Cibo wasn't elected as president of the wartime presidency at all, just as no president of the wartime presidency under war conditions was elected pursuant to the constitution, because given the war circumstances, it was necessary to replace the presidents of municipalities who might have fled the country or crossed over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, under the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the municipalities of Konjic, Jablanica, and Prozor did not represent any community of municipalities, did they? Just say if you know, if you don't know.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that municipalities are referred to in the constitution, that they are a subject matter that the constitution refers to directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. This was signed by Mr. Cibo, and this is -- refers to the exchange that we discussed a moment ago, which means the October exchange, and you say on the 19th of October, now take a look once again towards bottom Mr. Cibo is making a proposal that the exchange should take place one for one or in the ratio of one to one and this document was sent to the state commission and a letter seems to have been sent to Mr. Silajdzic as well. For the transcript I have to say that we don't have that letter now. Do you remember receiving this document from Mr. Cibo, the state commission? It was sent to the BH state commission for exchange.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that's right. If it was said that it was sent to the state commission, then it probably was sent to Sarajevo too. That's what I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we conclude then, Mr. Masovic, that it was the decision taken by the top political -- at the top political level down to the municipalities was that the exchange should be in the one-to-one ratio, although you say that that's not what happened. Is that what we can conclude?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the person who was authorised to negotiate the exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I highly respect your broad answers and your eloquence. The Prosecutor's going to help me with the microphone. I don't know what's happening to the microphone today it seems to be switching itself off on its own. Now from the two documents you were shown by my colleague Mr. Ibrisimovic and one that I've just shown you, one that you probably received as you yourself say, that quite obviously at that time the top leaders in the army and the political leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect to this exchange had the following position: That the exchange should take place in a one-to-one ratio and that later on you did not do that but the exchange took place as you explained it. That's all I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you consider being the political, army, and municipal leadership, because I consider --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, in this courtroom, as in any other courtroom for that matter, it is customary for me to ask questions, and I am saying that I consider the cabinet of the president of the presidency to be that and that it is Mr. Siber who was a member of the Supreme Command of the BH army, and I also consider that Mr. Cibo, the president of the three -- or, rather, the wartime presidency of the three municipalities, the political and army leadership when it comes to this exchange. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't. No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave that, Mr. Masovic, then. Quite obviously from the -- the documents speak for themselves and the Trial Chamber will be able to judge often the basis of the documents but you also said that the BH army arrested civilians who did not belong to the category of POWs and persons against whom criminal proceedings had been initiated but it was only individual incidents. Am I right? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, do we agree that an incident would be the following: For example, the arrest of a small number of civilians which were not among these other categories, didn't belong to any one of these other categories?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by a lesser number of civilians, a small number of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, you tell me what you think an incident means. If a hundred people are arrested, a hundred civilians, outside these categories, or if ten civilians were captured outside these categories.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that there were mass arrests which would incorporate dozens or hundreds of civilians. There were individual cases. One civilian, two civilians were deprived of their liberty outside legal provisions. That's the thing I do know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that the BH army arrested women and children, for example? In large numbers. Let's say more than ten.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge about that, except if they happened to have been women who were legally being prosecuted for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, how many women in the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, in the cantonal court in Sarajevo, if you can remember, were exchanged? How many women were exchanged? I worked there, and I took part in that process. So how many women -- a total of how many women in Sarajevo were legally prosecuted for crimes linked to the war events? Can you remember how many women?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't know about that, because I just dealt with one part of the persons who were captured, those who went for an exchange. Of course there were a larger number of persons who had been arrested who had nothing to do with the exchange process. So I can talk about that, although I don't know the figures, how many people were involved in the exchange process, who had been previously arrested and deprived of their liberty.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I'm interested in women and children now. Do you know that the BH army arrested civilians precisely to have them exchanged, and they weren't within one of those two categories that we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that the BH army, on the 27th and 28th of July, 1993, attacked the village of Doljani near Jablanica, and on that occasion they killed and massacred at least 43 Croats, amongst them civilians, women, children, and members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You never heard of that happening?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it wasn't within my remit, within my mandate. Let me repeat again. I don't know the purpose of you enumerating crimes which probably took place but which do not come under my terms of reference. So I can't talk about things that didn't have to do with the exchange of prisoners or killed persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I'm talking about the exchange of dead bodies, too, and you took part in that. And the purpose, I'll tell you what the purpose is. In the examination-in-chief, you claimed -- this isn't tu quoque, this is just an illustration that I want to show that what you said during the examination in chief as to how the BH army behaved was not quite true, and I'm going to show you that on the basis of documents. Now, when we come to Doljani and mentioning Doljani, take a look at the following document 2D 004 -- no, 588 is the document I'd like you to look at. It is the fourth document in my binder, one signed by a Mr. Rasim Delic. So once you've found it, please tell me. Take a look at it and tell me. And it's also on e-court.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say you know nothing about that, but never mind. I'm going to tell you that this is a letter written by Mr. Delic, the 6th Corps commander, who says that the President of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, received a letter from Tadeusz Mazowiecki, Special Rapporteur from the former Yugoslavia, claiming that in Prozor there was a massacre of at least 35 Bosnian Croats and that between the 27th and 29th of July, 1993, in the village of Doljani, near Jablanica, 22 Bosnian Croats were massacred. Now, here the commander of the armed forces of the BH army, the top military commander, two or three months after this massacre in Doljani is requesting from the 6th Corps command to inform him what happened, because that is something that Tadeusz Mazowiecki wants to know. Can you remember now, in view of the fact that the Presidency was informed of this and you had frequent contacts, can you remember having any knowledge whatsoever about this? And I'm referring to Doljani in particular, near Jablanica, and you'll see why I'm insisting on Doljani later on. Did you know about this and this letter?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you expect me to have knowledge of this, because from this document it does not follow that the state commission for the exchange of POWs was involved at all. It is obvious that the -- that a crime had taken place, that a crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, just say, "I don't know," and that's fine. I don't expect you to know about all the crimes committed in Bosnia. Just say you don't know and that will suffice and then I can move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know or did you -- do you know now that on that occasion, that is say, after the BH army attack on Doljani, in the Jablanica collection for POWs which was known as the Museum at Jablanica, that the Croatian population was taken out of the village and that they were incarcerated there? Do you know about that? I'm referring to July.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do know that in the Museum in Jablanica there were prisoners or evacuated persons. I'm using both terms, because there was a dispute about this and complaints from the HVO to the international -- ICRC who refused to record these persons as detainees or incarcerated persons but as people who had been evacuated and the HVO, rather, Mr. Pusic, on several occasions wrote letters of protest and sent them to the ICRC asking them to amend the status of those persons found in the Museum. Quite frankly, I don't know what their status was, so I can't say one way or another. I can't say they were prisoners or perhaps they were there of their own free will either.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you do agree with me nonetheless that in some collection centre no one would go there of their often free will?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't the case of a collection centre. It wasn't a collection centre at all as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right fine. Now, do you know that in this collection centre there might have been women and children?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Pusic several times at our meetings insisted upon the fact that those persons be evacuated to territory under HVO control, and I think he even said that there were some children too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Masovic, you said a moment ago that as far as you know, they were not in collection centres. Now, look at 6D 00035. It's the document with the yellow sticker, because that document has the status of exhibit. 6D 00035. And we're talking about Jablanica now. Just tell me when you've found it. It's up on e-court too on your screen.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Now, this is a BH army document. It is a document of the 6th Corps of the military police battalion, the military police company of Jablanica. The date is the 5th of August, 1993, and it says here the 6th Corps Military Police Battalion, subject, list of persons situated in the SRZ, and that is a collection centre of POWs, that that is the abbreviation used, the SRZ.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say whether that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, you can't, sir, fine. Do you know that the Museum in Jablanica was in fact that collection centre of POWs?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. Mr. Pusic spoke about that on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, then that's it. That's that. Do you want me to repeat it for the transcript? The list of persons situated in the SRZ of the Museum at Jablanica who were not members of the HVO. Now, Mr. Masovic, I'm going to ask you for the Trial Chamber's benefit, because perhaps the Trial Chamber didn't know who the women are and who the men are judging by the names of our part of the world, look at number 4 it says Dragica. That's a woman's name, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Number 10, another lady's name; right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Number 12, same thing?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Number 13?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Number 18?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Number 20?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right, 19 and 20. And finally, Mr. Masovic, unfortunately I don't have time, but on this list, and we can go through it if you want us to do so and if the Trial Chamber requests it, out of a total of 87 persons on that list who were not members of the HVO, which is something that the 6th Corps Military Police Battalion claims, there are 53 women on that list. There are 53 women, 53 women's names on that list. You knew nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about that, and I repeat, they were persons who you mentioned and were mentioned by Mr. Pusic who were from Doljani, evacuated --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and make pauses between question and answer, thank you, and turn on their microphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you answer just briefly, please, if you can. This is a document from the 6th Corps. Does it arise from this document that they are at the SRZ Museum, whatever that is?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So these are not people that may be at large somewhere. At least that's what arises from this document.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can -- I have to repeat and say that for the International Committee of the Red Cross their status was very clear. They were persons --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, sir. Mr. Masovic, but their status for the BiH army was that they were in the collection centre for prisoners of war. This is what I'm trying to say, and this arises from this document. If you don't know it, if you can't comment on it, just say so and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My previous answer has not been recorded in the transcript, so I would kindly ask you to allow me finish it. For the International Red Cross, their status was the status of persons that had to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then it is clear that there is a difference between the position of the International Red Cross and the BiH army. At least this is what arises from this document, because they were in the collection centre. And if the Red Cross says they had to be evacuated, it doesn't mean that they were not in the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are persistently trying to make me say that this is a collection centre, and we agreed previously this was the SRZ Museum in Jablanica. I said that I don't know what it means. I'm not saying that it is not what you're saying it is, but I don't know, and please do not try and make me say that this was a collection centre because I'm not going to answer in that way because I don't know. If I did know I would answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, you have answered. You have of told me that the Jablanica Museum was in actual fact a collection centre for the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Jablanica Museum for a certain while prisoners of war were kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very -- thank you very much. We're moving on. We have already established that in October you assisted an exchange in Konjic. You had lists during the exchange, and let me ask you this: Do you know, and I will allow that you don't, that in Konjic, in the general area of Konjic, that is, the BiH army arrested civilians, women and children, the whole families even?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be aware of that for a simple reason. They did not enter the process that I was in charge of. I'm talking about the process of exchanges of prisoners of war save for the two category that I would like to go back to. If you're talking about the specific exchange which took place on the 19th of October --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Konjic when it comes to the Croatian Defence Council, I was involved in the release of 309 members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is what I know. As for the rest, I can't be aware of anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, you have told us, and I'm not asking you this without any reason, I believe that I've laid the foundation for my next question, you said if the women and the children were arrested and especially the children and women against whom proceedings were not undergoing, if this was done by the BH army, it must have been an incident. That's why I'm asking you, did you have any information that this was not an incident and that's why I'm asking you whether you know that in Konjic there were arrests preceding the exchange and even women and children and whole families were arrested?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at 2D 00589. This is the last document in my binder save for the one that was added subsequently. Have the first page on e-court, but I believe that things will be easier for you if you find the hard copy in my binder. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a document issued on the 23rd of November, 1993, Konjic municipality, social services administration. This is obviously after the civilian population and troops had been exchanged and left Konjic. This list was compiled of imprisoned civilians in Konjic. Mr. Masovic, this list contains the names of 466 individuals. As you can see in the original document, certain names are accompanied by the word "with their families." There is also a large number of women. Let's just take, for example, the first page on which you will find the name of Milka Baric, a female, under number 5. Alenka Baric under 8. This is obviously two members of the same family; did you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't I've not seen this document before. This is a document by the HVO, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. By the HVO with the names and family names of individuals and whole families that hailed from the area of Konjic and that resided there up to this date. And were arrested before this date and before that they were civilians. You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you that really it absolutely doesn't make sense for the International Committee of the Red Cross not to register any of these individuals. I suppose that none of them were registered because there are a lot of names in this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... trying to avoid answering this question. Whenever the counsel asks you whether you knew whether the ABiH would arrest civilians whether they be women or children you answer by mentioning ICRC. That is not the question. The question is whether you knew the ABiH would arrest civilians. Just say whether you knew or you didn't. Don't try to involve the ICRC in this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have confirmed and I confirm it again that I have information about different parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina that people, civilians were arrested without any legal grounds for that I said it yesterday and I confirm it today that this was incidents, and this -- this was done by certain individuals or units of the BH army. This is what I said yesterday, and I repeat it today. In answer to this particular question, I have said and I repeated that this list was compiled by the HVO and that according to what I knew could -- is not credible. It is not reliable, because for such a large number of civilians, women, children, men, it is absolutely certain that this fact would have been recorded and made public. I'm sure that at least one of the international institutions who was tasked with recording such incidents and this was in October 1993, which I would like draw attention to, this was very far in the conflict, I'm sure this fact would have been recorded by the International Red Cross. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, if this document was drafted by the HVO, the previous one was drafted by the BiH army, and the previous document contains the names of 53 women. And if the 53 women had been incarcerated this would not constitute an incident. Do you agree with me? I have put a hypothetical question to you. If.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if. If they had been incarcerated, especially if they were females, if those were children, then 50 people would not constitute an incident. It would be much more than an incident, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, do you know that this Tribunal, The Hague Tribunal, issues a first instance judgement, IT-01-47-T on 15 March 2006 in the case Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura. Are you aware of that as a former attorney-at-law?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that a judgement was passed in this case, that there was a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that this decision establishes that the BiH army arrested civilians, women, children, which did not belong to the categories that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not had an occasion to read the sentence, the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at it together. Let's look at document 2D 00587, which is the third document in my binder. Just for the transcript, I would like to say that for the purpose of this cross-examination we have uploaded on e-court, i.e., we're going to use the document starting with count 1303 of the decision to count 1311 of this decision. Let's look at the decision together, Mr. Masovic, and would I particularly like to draw everybody's attention to these parts of the sentence are legally binding, because no appeal was lodged to these parts of the -- the decision either by the Prosecution or by the Defence. It says in count 1303, two detention centres were set up in Mehurici in Mehurici elementary school and in the smithy, known as Mehurici blacksmith shop. The school took in approximately 250 Bosnian Croat civilians between 6 June and 24 June 1993. Every part of this decision is very, very interesting. However, the time does not permit me what the Trial Chamber has established with this regard so could you please look at count 1306. This is on the following page in the English version and in the B/C/S version. It says here: "According to Witness Vinko Tadic, a Bosnian Croat civilian, a group of 13 or 14 armed soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms arrived in Konjska on the slope of Mount Vlasic early in the morning on 6 June 1993." I skip a sentence and I continue. "He stated that he was unable to identify the military unit to which the group of soldiers belonged, but he said that some of them wore green armbands with a badge marked 'MOS.'" It goes on: "The soldiers then assembled and arrested a group of villagers that included men, women and children." I skip a sentence and I go on: "Next on the order of a soldier whom they called Hadzija, the soldiers brought them to the village of Mehurici." I apologise. "On the order of a soldier named Hadzija, the soldiers brought them to the village of Mehurici. When they arrived in Mehurici the villagers were taken to Mehurici elementary school and installed in its sports room." Please look at the part of this decision under 1307 on the following page. It says: "As indicated previously in the judgement on 8 June 1993, following a fresh outbreak of fighting between the HVO and the ABiH, in Maline 306th Brigade Military Police escorted a column of approximately 250 prisoners consisting of Bosnian Croat civilians and the HVO soldiers who had surrendered previously to Mehurici elementary school." Under 1308 it says: "Most of the detainees assembled in the school sports room were elderly people, women and children, including very young children and pregnant women." I skip a sentence. And it goes on: "Some witnesses stated that the civilians were locked up in the school in order to protect them from the Mujahedin given the proximity of their camp in Poljanica, or to safeguard the civilian population in view of the intensifying fighting in the region." We can look at the footnote. This was stated by Remzija Siljeg, Munir Karic, who are obviously Bosniaks and did not fall in the category of the detainees who were all Croats. Wouldn't that be correct? It goes on to say in the judgement that there were some witnesses who spoke about the interest of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to exchange these prisoners for -- for the prisoners -- Muslim prisoners captured by the HVO. I'm just going to refer to one more count in the judgement, 1310, which says that individuals and especially men who were detained in the gym were physically ill-treated. Mr. Masovic, you said that you were not aware of this judgement, but let me ask you whether you heard of these events during the war or during the exchanges? Did you hear of the events that had taken place in territory of Zenica regarding the incarceration of Croatian civilians?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians that are mentioned in this judgement and the reason for their stay in the school is not clear from what you have just read out to me, because there are witnesses who say one thing, and there are also others who say something else, were never the subject of exchanges. One of the witnesses, as I can see, or more of them say that they may have been incarcerated with a view to being exchanged. I wouldn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, you have left me with the room to ask you this because you have said expressly that the policy of the government in Sarajevo was to send these two categories for exchange. You said that any arrest of people outside of these two categories fall under the motion of incident. I'm putting it to you that the people who were arrested here were also pregnant women and children who were certainly not -- did not fall within those two categories. I'm asking you whether you knew anything about that during your mandate. The Trial Chamber has established that, and the Honourable Judge Antonetti was the Presiding Judge in this case. He has established that for a fact. I'm asking you what you know about that as a witness sitting before this Trial Chamber today?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: This category of civilians was not part of the mandate of the commission that I was in charge of and also it doesn't arise from what you have just said or at least I don't see it, you are more familiar with the judgement, I see it for the first time, but I don't see why these people would have been kept in the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic -- Mr. Masovic, under wartime conditions is there a single logical reason for a pregnant child -- woman and child to be found in prisoner anywhere?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Now, I have to wind up, and I'm almost done. Now, you don't have to agree with some of the things I'm going to say, but from the documents I've shown you, does it follow that - this is my question - that the BH army arrested civilians among whom women and children. From the documents we've seen. I'm not asking you on the basis of your knowledge but on the basis of the documents we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat, what I know is that that was at the level of incidents. They were incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. I haven't got more time to go into all this. I just have an hour at my disposal, so that will suffice. According to the number of arrested persons, from the documents we've seen, from the different places where they were arrested, can you tell us now, on the assumption that these documents are true and correct, that they were incidents or were they something more than just an incident?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents don't speak of arrested persons or rather incarcerated persons. In the document all that is mentioned - you said that the Croatian Defence document made this document in Ljubuski in November and that this refers to persons who imprisoned, 400 and something.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I hope you're not going to deny that from the judgement I read out that there were two detention centres. And I've just quoted that from the document, the document the BH army compiled, how many there were. Just take this one here, this judgement. They are detention centres. You don't have to answer my question. You can say yes, no, or I don't know, or you don't have to answer, but I haven't got the time to go back to the arguments that I put forward which are incontestable when it comes to the judgement. Your position is clear to me. I'm quite clear on your position. All I'm asking you is does that follow from these documents? You can say that it doesn't or that it does or that you don't know. Let me repeat according to the number of persons incarcerated and the different places that this happened and according to the documents I showed you can this be considered to be just a mere incident, the arrest of women and children, would -- would you consider those to be incidents? Or something more?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documents that you've shown me, it clearly follows that in all these cases they were not arrests as you state. So in the SRZ Museum Jablanica --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. I don't have any time to go into all that. You gave me an answer and that will suffice. Mr. Masovic, in the judgement which I quoted a moment ago it says that the BH army, among other things, arrested civilians for an exchange. Can you confirm that that's what it says in the judgement there, that that was what a certain number of witnesses also claimed? Say you can't confirm it, you can.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just tell me -- I'm not sure what paragraph you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, forget my question. The paragraph exists, the judgement exists, the Trial Chamber will deal with it. I think that's more important than your answer and my question, but I want to ask you one more thing. You spoke about the HVO policy. I don't have a single document. It's a short topic, so let's take it slowly. You spoke of the HVO policy to evacuate civilians from the area controlled by the BH army and areas which were not -- or, rather, persons who were not detained, not incarcerated. I don't want to mention any other -- any of the accused, but you said that you gained the impression that that was HVO policy, that they wanted to evacuate the Croats from areas where Croats were not incarcerated; right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Masovic, is it normal on the basis of your experience for civilians to wish to leave the territory which was taken control of by the enemy army in which their compatriots were arrested and where crimes might have been committed? Is it normal for civilians, civilians who consider themselves to be enemy ones because under -- in quotation marks. Is it normal that they wish to leave the territory that was not controlled by their side?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about this in a different context yesterday and an attempt --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, look at my context and answer me within my context. We spent the whole war in Sarajevo, you and I. Is it normal? I just wants you to confirm this, if you will, that civilians want to leave a territory that was taken control of by the enemy army? That's how the Bosniaks left and the Serbs left and the Croats left. Isn't that normal? Is that normal for civilians to leave the territory that has been taken control of by the enemy army?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not normal if that happens through the process of the exchange of those civilians. Then it's not normal. Under different conditions it would be normal, in my opinion, regardless of the territory, enemy or not, that civilians try to avoid war operations, but it's not normal that that will should be done through the commission for the exchange of POWs -- or prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It seems to me that the interpreters have gained allies among the technicians, so when we speed up the microphones seem to be switched off, but let's look at the Doljani situation, where quite obviously a massacre had taken place and Mr. Delic wrote about that, too, in his letter. When we look at the question -- the instance of Konjic where there was an exchange of HVO members in large numbers and Jablanica in that Museum where there were members of the HVO and some other citizens. And when we look at the case of Zenica from this judgement and the broader area around Zenica, and if we remember Bugojno where 21 Croats were killed, we know that, and we know that they were very prominent Croats, they were leaders of the Croatian ethnicity in Bugojno, is it then the legitimate right of civilians living in that territory to wish to leave when incidents like this are taking place, not to say crimes - or let me say crimes - and when their compatriots are being arrested? Would that be normal?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's an individual decision, and that's what happened in wartime. Some people left the territory for those and other reasons, for hunger and fear, out of fear, or some other reason, the possibility of finding themselves in other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's take fear, one of the factors you mentioned. Was that one of the basic motives that moved a large number of individuals to move out? I'm not talking about individuals. Foca -- not Srebrenica, other territories from which the Bosniaks were expelled by the Serbs. Was the -- was fear a legitimate reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your last question, Ms. Nozica, because we've got another two counsel to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but our Defence will have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you. Your Honour, I just have two or three more questions, and I've been given permission from the Coric Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. You've been given some time. How much?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll need a total of five minutes, which was what I was given. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no questions for this witness, so if my colleague Ms. Nozica needs a few more minutes, she can have our time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I'm going to ask you this now, you were asked it during the examination-in-chief: Why did the Croatian civilians, can you tell us why the Croatian civilians from Catici went to take refuge in the base of the French Battalion? Did they do that out of fear? Did they leave their homes out of fear? You don't know?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Mr. Masovic, when somebody leaves their home and goes to the French Battalion base, let's forget that they were Croats just for a moment. Can you and I assume that people do that kind of thing out of fear?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't want to speculate about things that I don't know. I have absolutely no knowledge that. All I can do is to assume and guess, and I don't think that that is what is required here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, but I'm sorry, but I get the feeling that you are inviting the witness to speculate what other people might have for motives for doing this and that and I wonder whether this gives a solid factual basis to the Chamber. You want him to say what -- what you want him to say, but you ask him to speculate. What do you think other people's -- why do other people do this and that? Every one of us can answer that question. I don't know why this witness should add anything to the knowledge of the Chamber if he makes that kind of assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, it is my task and duty to try and extract from the witness what I want to extract. That is the business of cross-examination. If the witness says he knows nothing about it, I won't insist further. But I did ask him about something that would be considered to be normal. If the witness says he doesn't want to speculate, I'll move on. That's sufficient for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now my last question, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask a follow-up question. When people would be liberated, released, you and the members of your commission, would you meet with the people who had just been released? Would you discuss with them about what had happened, what they had experienced, why they had been arrested, what they were intending to do in the future? Did you have this kind of contact? I mean, between you and the members of your commission and the released people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We focused exclusively on seeing whether those prisoners who had been free -- freed knew about other prisoners who possibly stayed on in the camps or prisons from which these others had come or in some other prison or camp where they stayed from time to time. All other questions, questions about their future, who mistreated them, why they were arrested in the first place, all these other questions were the task of other state organs to delve into, mostly the police, the military police if it was POWs and prosecutors if they had -- if they were in serious violation of international humanitarian law. We in the commission just focused on their knowledge about the names of people who stayed on, who remained in the camps or prisons after they had left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, you had contacts with the people who had been released. However, those who were released, did they at any time tell you that -- that when they had been captured it was -- they were captured because the other side would also capture people, and there were between the warring parties exchange of prisoners? One side would take some people, the other one would do the same, and then they would make phone calls in order to exchange prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not ask them things like that. When we were interested in was whether there were any more prisoners in the camps and whether these prisoners had taken part in burying other prisoners or had anything to do with the places where these others were buried and where we could find the bodily remains of the prisoners who might have been killed. Now, all your questions, Your Honour, all the questions you've just asked me, are questions that they asked or -- or, rather, the police, the military police, the prosecutors asked them immediately after they left the camps and prisons. Quite literally sometimes directly from the place of exchange, took them to the police station or the policemen would come to these locations if we were dealing with a larger number of people released, or they would go to the schools or gymnastics halls where the released prisoners were collected, and then the officials would take statements of that nature from the prisoners who had been released.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, now, you've just told the Trial Chamber that you were a Member of Parliament. You're a -- you have been politically active for some time, so now I'd like to ask you a question which is broader and relates to your political knowledge and other knowledge. We discussed the situation, a hypothetical situation, according to which the population finding themselves on a territory occupied by the enemy army does its best to leave the area, I would like to ask you in your opinion - if you can answer do it, so if you cannot, say you cannot - would it be the duty of the authorities to which these civilians belonged to protect them and to try to put them up in an area where they would be safe and secure? Would that be the duty of the authorities regardless of which authorities they would be?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me make myself clearer. We had a few interruptions but I'd like to take you back to the civilians' departure from the areas occupied, for instance, by an enemy army, and I'm asking you the following: In your opinion, is it the duty of the authorities to whom those civilians belong, those civilians who stayed on in the territory, is it the duty of the authorities to try and relocate them somewhere else where they would be safer, move them to an area where they would be safer if they are in jeopardy?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about an international conflict or what? I don't understand what you want, what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I believe that to an extent the question is asking for a legal opinion, the witness is not competent to address this particular issue in terms of the responsibilities, legal responsibilities of the authorities. I think certainly he's competent to talk about his experience in the release issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, the witness is an attorney-at-law. He has been a member of a large number of legal commissions in his country, even of a constitutional commission. So if there is one individual who is able to state a view with regard to a sort of problem of legal nature, he's the one. So please proceed, Ms. Nozica, but maybe you might rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, according to your experience and legal knowledge, would it be logical for the authorities to try and relocate the citizens somewhere safe if they are in the territory under the control of the enemy army and as such threatened in some way? Wouldn't that be the obligation of that government?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring of to the concrete conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina or speaking generally?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the concrete conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would the government have to have done that in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government in Bosnia-Herzegovina is one and only, the government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I didn't want to open that subject, but let me tell you this. There was just one government and you asked me to agree with you?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my positive answer to your question would be this: That government in Sarajevo was duty-bound to make sure to protect all the civilians that were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, did they succeed? Did they succeed to protect everybody?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How many Serbs and Croats in Sarajevo were killed and taken to the front line and exchanged how many such persons were there, do you know? Did the government in Sarajevo -- in Sarajevo where the headquarters of the government was to -- were they successful at protecting Croats in November 1993 when the leadership of the HVO were arrested? Were they afraid and did they leave Sarajevo because of that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not done by the government in Sarajevo but the Serbian government in Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Zec [phoen] incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who arrested him in Sarajevo, Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the government. After --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm one of many perhaps who is struggling to follow this dialogue, but it seems to me it's getting beyond the scope of the direct examination or at least beyond the scope of what's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're talking about the Serbs authorities here, and so again if I could just finish, I'd like to say that the exchange is happening extremely quickly, and it seems to be going in a direction that doesn't mean anything to me and so I'm objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The exchange is rather quick and they do need to slow down, but what is quite evident today is that the gentleman is obviously biased and that he is one-sided, and I think it is relevant, because what Ms. Nozica is showing is the bias of this gentleman and we're going to be arguing that at least with some of his answers that this Trial Chamber should disregard. That's the purpose. That's why it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, counsel's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Look, we have to have a break. We will have a 20-minute break, and after the break around 6.00, Ms. Nozica will have to finish because then we will have Mr. Kovacic and possibly some additional -- some redirect from Mr. Stringer. We shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing's resumed. Mr. Stringer, you were on your feet, and I interrupted you. What did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I had made an objection at the end of the proceedings. I've said what I wanted to say, and I have nothing to add at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Ms. Nozica, are you done?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, but I will be done very soon. To Mr. Stringer's objection, I would like to say that on direct Mr. Masovic mentioned Mr. Zelic, and that is why I went back to that question, and now I would like to draw my cross-examination to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, you've told us that you recognised only the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo; is that correct? You said that immediately before our last break.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo as the government of an internationally recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I lived in Sarajevo together with you, and that is also the only government that I recognise myself, but I'm asking you now whether you are familiar with the fact that the international community recognised the government of the HZ HB and Republika Srpska, that the international community negotiated with the two of them, that the government in Sarajevo also negotiated with these two entities, to call them that. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you are referring to the constitutional matter, and I am now referring to the constitution as well, and who negotiated with whom, who recognised whom, I really don't know. I was not familiar with those negotiations. If you'd asked me about the constitutional order of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would say this was the government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you that because you have already stated it. We will not go into that matter. Finally, when we're talking about the matter of recognition, or factual recognition as you put it, you will be familiar with the fact that representative of the HZ HB signed the Washington Agreement. Are you aware of that? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you're referring to. Can you please be more precise? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The representative of the HZ HB. Do you know who signed the Dayton agreement on behalf of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was signed by Presidents Izetbegovic, Tudjman, and Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Zubak, as a representative of the HZ HB, also participated in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he participated but I don't know what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You don't know. Thank you, Mr. Masovic. I have just received a suggestion from my colleague. Tell me, Mr. Masovic, just one more question, when you were talking about the discovery of the Goranci grave, you said that Mrs. Sonja Mulac called you - Interrupt me if I'm not interpreting your answer correctly - and that you said about a dead body she recognised a uniform and she concluded this might be a Bosniak and that's when she called you and that's when you arrived there. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that somebody from the Serb commission suggested to her that those were not Serb soldiers as they originally thought but, rather, that they were Bosniaks, and that's when I went there on the following day to assist the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How can you recognise somebody as being a Bosniak by their uniform? What was that Bosniak army, and what uniforms did it wear? I'm asking you this because you are insisting on the fact that there was only the government in Sarajevo covering the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that it was supposed to be the government or the authority representing all of the citizens. I'm asking you how could you have assumed on the basis of the uniform that the person buried in that uniform was a Bosniak; what kind of a uniform would that have been? Was that the uniform of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Bosniaks. I'm talking about members of the BiH army, some of whom were not even Bosniaks but they wore the uniforms of the BiH army. One of the ten identified members of the BiH army from Vranica was not Bosniak. His father is Serb and his mother is a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, we still have the transcript before us. On page 15, page 82 -- line 82 [as interpreted], you say in answer to my question that Sonja Mulac called you because she had recognised one person as being Bosniak. I'm asking you this: Do you believe, yourself -- when she called you did you believe that members of the BH army were supposed to be Bosniaks, all of them? Is that what you implied when you said that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that during your cross-examination, if I said that those were Bosniaks, it was not correct. I believe that in my testimony yesterday - I believe but I'm not sure - that after the uniform of the BiH army was recognised, I went there to assist in the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I remember that you said that the uniform told you that it was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible to tell who's who just by the uniform. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I agree with you. I agree with you when you say that.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about ethnicity, but obviously it is possible to recognise the army that that uniform belonged to. And based on the uniform, we were able to tell the army that the victim belonged to without knowing whether that person was a Serb, a Croat, or a Bosniak or somebody else from Vranica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Masovic. I agree with you. That's what -- why I found your yesterday's answer strange.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to file an oral request in keeping with your decision of 10 May 2007. I'm referring to paragraphs 11 and 12 to allow Mr. Praljak to put questions to the witness himself, and I'm basing this request on the fact that the topics in question were -- have been studied by General Praljak after the war. He was in charge of the research of that particular topic, the topic of prisoners of war and victims in various locations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He has collected all the publicly available information. He analysed that information, and he has published the information in a booklet that was published in 2006. I believe that he possesses a lot of knowledge about the topic, which makes him competent in terms of the definition of extraordinary circumstances that is referred to in the decision that was passed on the 10th of May, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the title of this booklet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title of the booklet -- you have it, Your Honours, before you. "Croatian victims during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina," which provides an overview of various locations and events, and the booklet is based on the existing literature. I would kindly ask the usher to -- [In English] Usher. I gave it to him. Okay. You will find -- you will find that book enclosed, Your Honour. Earlier we have used some similar material which was then only the draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have two objections. The first is that in our view this subject matter and this witness do not fall within any of the exceptions identified by the Trial Chamber in its ruling. There's nothing particularly exceptional about this topic, and particularly in view of the fact that it may be something that the General has studied or any of us has possibly studied. It doesn't fall within the terms of the Trial Chamber's order, certainly not the sort of military expertise, military aspects that the Trial Chamber has allowed General Praljak to conduct examinations on in the past. Secondly, I've got a book here for which I don't have a translation. I see that it is largely maps, but it's not just maps. It's a lot of other things, including photographs, diagrams, commentary for which I do not have a translation, and that's another basis for the objection. So it's our submission that this is not a situation which Mr. Praljak, especially in view of the fact that he's got such competent counsel, needs to himself conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may respond to one part of my learned friend's objection, the initial part in which my learned friend claims that this argument is not in keeping with the provisions of your order. I believe that this argument does not hold its ground. You said that -- in your order that exceptional circumstances may arise in two occasions, if the accused himself participated in an event or he is particularly competent to discuss this issue. This is the topic of victims, which relates to the topic of exchanges in the unfortunate war. I believe that is very specific area, bearing in mind the rumours, the policy, the propaganda goals that existed on both sides, and General Praljak has -- has invested a lot of effort to study just one of the segments of this topic and research that based on facts. Maybe General Praljak can supplement my argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer said that he did not have the translation. Would you mind reading out the first page just to have a idea as to whether he has special knowledge in this field when it comes to missing people. But I can lend you mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I have not got a copy, but I believe it is forthcoming. [In English] Maybe Mr. Praljak, since he has a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since Mr. Praljak has the book, he can read the first page. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you very much for the time given to me. I will briefly explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. Sorry. You haven't been granted anything yet. There is a discussion among the Judges on the Bench. I wanted to know what the title was. Would you mind reading it out and the interpreters will translate, will interpret into the languages we need. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to explain and say that there are other topics that the witness mentioned before your decision and that concern the things that I know of, and that is the HVO, whether Mostar was under siege or not, the arrest of Mr. Zelic, and so on and so forth. So it is not just this. And the title of the book is literally this and I quote: "Crimes committed by some members of the BiH army (Muslim units) over Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991" -- or, rather, "from 1991 to 1995." The connection between this topic and this gentleman is the fact that the mortal remains of some of these people have still been missing and I would like to ask him about Grabovica and ask him whether mortal remains of the people from Grabovica, how much he knows about that, which locations have been investigated, which locations haven't been investigated, what number are we talking about and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After deliberations, we authorise you to ask questions but only related to specific situations. For instance, with relation to research on Croats who were allegedly killed by members of the BiH army. So anything that is in direct connection to your own work, specific cases without digressing any which way. So you just have 30 minutes, so that there is at least 15 minutes for redirect. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I'd like to ask you the following: My questions, pursuant to the Court's instructions, will be brief, precise, I hope very clear and to the point. So would you please answer likewise, yes, no, or I don't know. All the explanations that you had you gave to the Prosecutor, and if Their Honours would like to ask you for additional explanations, they will do so. You are the witness here and I have been given permission to examine some of the assertions you made during the examination-in-chief. You said that of the 70 persons who were the subject of the exchange, HVO soldiers [indiscernible] in Mostar, the helicopter problem, that there were two or three members of the Croatian army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When I say members of the Croatian army, does that mean that they were members of the Croatian army who came to fight within the HVO, or were they members of some Croatian unit in the area, in the territory and were then captured? Which? So the question is how do you know that they were actually members of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the report that came in from the prison. Those two who were in Eastern Mostar in prison, it's said that they were members of the Croatian army and not members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you only know it on the basis of the report. You know nothing more about that. You don't know which unit they belonged to; right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that one of them was from Rijeka. I don't know where the other one was from, and I know their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was one Igor Kapor?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that Igor Kapor was a member of the 4th Guard's Brigade with headquarters in Split?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Fine. Now do you know that Igor Kapor, travelling to Kiseljak where he was going to be married, was arrested in Jablanica and transferred to Mostar where he was in prison until your agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that there were body -- the bodies of nine members of the Croatian army there. Do you also know that from the report, from a report?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that on the basis of the minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exchange --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you said that Igor Kapor was about to get married. Do you know that? Are you sure? Do you have any evidence? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We have full evidence of that, and if need be we can bring the man in to testify. It was a man who was going there to get married, and he spent one year after that in prison in Mostar but he was going to Kiseljak to get married. That's something that Mr. Petkovic knows and I think we can all testify first-hand when my turn comes, as you say. And we can bring the man in too, depending on the amount of time we have. May I be allowed to continue? Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So these nine men, do you know whether they were -- died or were killed or whatever you want to call it, that there was a unit to which they belonged, or from the Croatian army did they go as volunteers to fight in the HVO because they were from the area just like I was? Do you know about any of that? Or do you just base your knowledge on the report you received?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
